title: Maximum Points You Can Obtain from Cards
description: Brute force to optimized: resumming every front/back split versus reframing as total-minus-minimum over a fixed-size sliding window.

content.title: Maximum Points You Can Obtain from Cards

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

There are several cards arranged in a row, each with a point value given by the array cardPoints. In one step, you may take exactly one card from either the beginning or the end of the row. You must take exactly k cards total. Return the maximum total points achievable.

blocks.caption: Taking k cards from the ends always leaves behind one contiguous middle block

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","An integer array cardPoints, and an integer k (the exact number of cards to take, from either end)"],["Output","The maximum total points achievable by taking exactly k cards, one at a time, from either end"],["Goal","Find this without trying every possible sequence of front/back choices"],["Constraints","1 <= cardPoints.length <= 10^5; 1 <= cardPoints[i] <= 10^4; 1 <= k <= cardPoints.length"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["Taking exactly k cards from either end always leaves a single CONTIGUOUS block behind","Reframe \"maximize what's taken\" as \"minimize the one leftover middle block\""],["The leftover block always has a FIXED size (n - k)","A fixed-size sliding window sliding across the array, tracking the minimum sum"],["Total points are fixed regardless of choices","Precompute the total once, then subtract the minimum window sum found"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem
Given cardPoints and an integer k, taking cards one at a time from either end of the row for exactly k total picks, find the maximum achievable total.

blocks.title: Analogy: Eating From Both Ends of a Row of Snacks
blocks.text: Like eating snacks from either end of a row, taking exactly k bites total. Whatever isn't eaten always forms one single contiguous stretch in the middle, so maximizing what's eaten is the same as finding the least tasty stretch to leave behind.

blocks.caption: The best score is the total minus the smallest possible leftover block of size n - k

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: cardPoints = [1,2,3,4,5,6,1], k = 3

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Total of all cards: 1+2+3+4+5+6+1 = 22","Total: 22","This is fixed regardless of which cards are taken"],["Smallest leftover block of size 7-3=4: [1,2,3,4] sums to 10","Minimum leftover: 10","Leaving this block behind means taking the cards 5,6,1 (the last 3), plus nothing from the front"],["Answer","12","22 (total) - 10 (min leftover) = 12"]]}

blocks.text: Example: cardPoints = [2,2,2], k = 2

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Total: 2+2+2 = 6. Smallest leftover block of size 3-2=1: any single 2","Minimum leftover: 2","Every possible leftover block of size 1 has the same value here"],["Answer","4","6 (total) - 2 (min leftover) = 4"]]}

blocks.text: Edge case: k equals the full array length
When every single card must be taken, there is no leftover block at all, and the answer is simply the total sum of cardPoints.
5. How Should We Think?
Before trying every possible split between taking from the front and taking from the back, notice that whatever is left behind always forms one single contiguous stretch.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Taking some cards from the front and the rest from the back always leaves exactly one contiguous block of un-taken cards in the middle, whose size is always exactly (n - k), regardless of the front/back split chosen.

Observation 2: Since the total of all cards is fixed, maximizing the taken total is exactly equivalent to minimizing the leftover block's sum.

Observation 3: The leftover block always has the SAME fixed size (n - k), so this becomes finding the minimum-sum window of that fixed size anywhere in the array.

Observation 4: Slide a fixed-size window of size (n - k) across the array, tracking the minimum sum seen, then subtract it from the precomputed total.

Reframing "maximize what's taken from both ends" as "minimize the one leftover middle block" turns an apparently combinatorial front/back choice problem into a single fixed-size sliding window minimum search.
This is the fixed-size sliding window pattern applied to find a MINIMUM sum, then subtracted from a precomputed total, rather than tracking a maximum directly.
6. Brute Force Solution
For every possible split of how many cards to take from the front versus the back, compute the total directly.
Step by step algorithm

items: For every possible number of cards taken from the front (from 0 to k), take the remaining (k minus that number) cards from the back.
Sum the front-taken and back-taken cards directly for each split, tracking the maximum total found.

codes.python:
def max_score(card_points, k):
    n = len(card_points)
    best = 0
    for taken_from_front in range(k + 1):
        taken_from_back = k - taken_from_front
        front_sum = sum(card_points[:taken_from_front])
        back_sum = sum(card_points[n - taken_from_back:]) if taken_from_back > 0 else 0
        best = max(best, front_sum + back_sum)
    return best


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(max_score([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 1], 3))

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every possible front/back split (k+1 total splits) is tried explicitly, since the split alone determines exactly which cards get taken.
frontSum and backSum are each summed directly per split, rather than incrementally, since this brute force does not yet share work between splits.
best only ever increases, tracking the highest total found across every split.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Every possible front/back split is checked directly, so the correct maximum is always found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(k squared) in the worst case, since each of the (k+1) splits sums up to k cards directly.
Space: O(1) extra.

Limitation: resumming the front and back portions from scratch for every split ignores that shifting the split by one only moves a single card between the taken and leftover groups, which can be tracked incrementally instead.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force resums the front and back groups from scratch for every split. Instead, reframe the problem entirely: whatever is left behind always forms one contiguous block of fixed size (n - k). Precompute the total sum once, then slide a fixed-size window of size (n - k) across the array, tracking its minimum sum. The answer is simply the total minus that minimum. Sliding the window costs O(1) per shift, since only one element enters and one leaves at a time.

Compute the total sum once. Build an initial window of size (n - k) starting at index 0, summing its contents. Slide the window one position at a time, adding the entering element and subtracting the leaving one, tracking the minimum sum seen. Subtract this minimum from the total for the final answer.
9. Optimized Solution
Precompute the total once, then slide a fixed-size window of size (n - k) to find the minimum leftover block.
Dry run for cardPoints = [1,2,3,4,5,6,1], k = 3 (window size = 7 - 3 = 4)

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: total (22) - minimum window (10) = 12, matching the expected answer.

codes.python:
def max_score(card_points, k):
    n = len(card_points)
    window_size = n - k                                                     # size of the single leftover middle block
    total = sum(card_points)
    if window_size == 0:
        return total                                                        # taking every single card, nothing is left behind
    window_sum = sum(card_points[:window_size])
    min_window = window_sum
    for right in range(window_size, n):
        window_sum += card_points[right] - card_points[right - window_size]  # slide the leftover block forward by one
        min_window = min(min_window, window_sum)
    return total - min_window


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(max_score([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 1], 3))

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), one pass to compute the total plus one pass to slide the fixed-size window.
Space: O(1) extra.
Why This Works

Every valid way of taking k cards from the ends corresponds to exactly one contiguous leftover block of size (n - k) somewhere in the array (the block simply shifts as the front/back split changes), so scanning every possible position of that fixed-size block covers every valid taking strategy exactly once.

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: windowSize is computed once as (n - k), representing the fixed size of whatever gets left behind.
The initial window is summed directly over its first windowSize elements before the sliding loop begins.
Each slide step adds exactly one entering element and removes exactly one leaving element, keeping the update O(1) per shift.

blocks.text: 10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Time","Space","Notes"],"rows":[["Brute force (resum every front/back split)","O(k squared)","O(1) extra","Each split independently resums its front and back portions"],["Optimized (total minus minimum fixed-size window)","O(n)","O(1) extra","A single pass slides the fixed-size leftover-block window across the whole array"]]}

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways
Reframing "maximize what's taken from both ends" as "minimize the one contiguous leftover block" is the key insight that turns this into a standard fixed-size sliding window problem.
Common mistakes

items: Trying to simulate every possible sequence of front/back picks directly, rather than recognizing the leftover block is always a single contiguous stretch.
Forgetting the window_size = 0 edge case when k equals the full array length, where there is no leftover block at all.
Resumming the window from scratch at every slide position instead of maintaining a running sum incrementally.

blocks.text: Interview tips

items: State the "leftover block is always contiguous and fixed-size" reframing out loud before coding, since it's the single insight that makes this problem tractable.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Take exactly k items from either end of a row to maximize a total" points toward reframing as "minimize the one fixed-size contiguous block left behind", then sliding a fixed-size window.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you also report exactly which cards to take? Track the leftover window's start index at the moment the minimum is updated, then take everything outside that range.
What if cards could only be taken from the front, never the back? This collapses to a simple fixed-size prefix sum, no sliding window needed at all.

How would this generalize to taking cards from k different ends of a circular arrangement? The fixed-size leftover-block reframing still applies, but the array would need to be treated as circular (e.g., via doubling) first.

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: A fixed-size sliding window problem tracking a minimum instead of a maximum, in the same family as Maximum Average Subarray I and Grumpy Bookstore Owner, but solved indirectly via total-minus-minimum rather than directly.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(k squared) time, O(1) space.
Optimized (total minus minimum fixed-size window): O(n) time, O(1) space.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: Fixed-size sliding window, applied to find a minimum sum, subtracted from a precomputed total
Core Idea: Whatever cards are left behind always form one contiguous block of fixed size (n - k); minimizing that block maximizes what's taken
Time: O(n)
Space: O(1)
Most Important Observation: Maximizing points taken from both ends is equivalent to minimizing the one contiguous leftover middle block
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: Total minus the smallest fixed-size window
